prize_parts.citation: for the invention of the optical lattice clock based on the magic-wavelength condition and its development to a fractional uncertainty of 10^-18

statement.case_for: I have moved from B018 to B012. The magic-wavelength lattice is a physical idea, not just a better number: it removes first-order light shifts, Doppler and recoil effects while keeping thousands of atoms in the measurement, and that is what took optical clocks to about 10^-18. Independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE) have reproduced and compared clocks at that level, and the systematic shifts are understood quantitatively. That is the standard of verification I look for as a theorist: theory and measurement close the loop, and many-body and spin-exchange effects in the clock are now treated in detail. The credit is also the cleanest on the shortlist, with Katori for the concept and first demonstration and Ye for taking it to the accuracy frontier. The chair's first question asks what separates this from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes. Those honoured the enabling tool and a neighbouring single-ion route. A citation that names the magic-wavelength lattice and the 10^-18 regime, and does not credit clocks in general, honours a distinct, verified achievement. Kroll's argument, that this is a physics idea that happens to be an instrument, persuaded me in round 1 and still does.
statement.case_against: The overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes is real, and a colleague can fairly call this a maturing refinement of a recognised programme rather than a new phenomenon. The fundamental-physics payoff (varying constants, dark matter, the redefinition of the second) is still prospective, so the citation must rest on the demonstrated clock performance, not on promised discoveries. Credit beyond two names is open to challenge: Lemonde, Ludlow, Takamoto, Bloom and the PTB, NIST and SYRTE groups made important contributions, and ion clocks reached similar accuracy by another route. I also give up what I valued in B018, a new class of quantum matter with theory and experiment matched. B012 is, as Pearce says, partly attractive because it offends nobody. I do not think that is a good reason in itself, and I support it because I could not fix B018's attribution problem, not because it is the safe option.

responses.point: Johansson ranks B018 as the strongest alternative but not as his lead, because the HgTe proposal by Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang made the Konig experiment possible, Zhang is deceased, and a Kane-Mele-Molenkamp trio leaves out that proposal.
responses.response: This is the point that has moved me most. I had treated the omission as a flaw that the three-person limit forced on us. Having thought about it again, I cannot find a way to cite the prediction, the HgTe proposal and the first observation within three names without cutting either Kane or Mele or Molenkamp. A citation that credits the experiment to Molenkamp while omitting the proposal that told him which material to grow is not defensible, and it would also be awkward that the proposer cannot be honoured. Your reasoning therefore persuades me, and I withdraw B018 as my lead. I keep it as an alternative, since the physics is not in doubt.

responses.point: Mehlig says that B018 is the safer choice on maturity but that the 2016 prize on topological phases partly covers its ground, and that its attribution problem is as hard as the Cao problem for B022. He also argues that flat bands and correlated insulators do not depend on the pairing mechanism.
responses.response: I accept the symmetry you draw between our two candidates. After the first round I cannot claim that B018's attribution is cleaner than B022's. I also take your point that a citation limited to flat bands and correlated insulating states would not depend on the unresolved pairing. My remaining concern with B022 is not the physics but timing. Several of us still treat the field as a few years early, and Cao and the early moire theorists fall outside any three names. I would revisit it in a later cycle. I do not agree that it should lead now, but your argument leaves it as a serious future candidate and I keep it as an alternative.

responses.point: Kroll answers the novelty objection by arguing that the magic-wavelength idea is a physics idea that happens to be an instrument, and that the quantitative result is unambiguous. He lists the Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow and Bloom contributions and the JILA connection in his own history.
responses.response: I agree with the first part and have used it in my own case. I also thank you for disclosing the Boulder year and think the committee can note it as adjacent, not as a conflict. On the credit, I think the committee should keep the citation narrow: the magic-wavelength lattice clock and its 10^-18 realisation, with Katori and Ye as the two names. That wording does not claim to represent the whole programme and it leaves Lemonde, Ludlow and others as contributors rather than unrecognised discoverers. I would like an external expert report on the lattice-clock community's view of priority before the vote.

responses.point: Pearce, the chair, asks that those who prefer other candidates say what would move them, and notes that B012 attracts consensus in part because it offends nobody, which is not the same as being the most important candidate.
responses.response: What moved me is attribution, not the count of supporters, and I agree support counts should not decide this. I do not rank the clock above topological matter on scientific importance. I rank it above B018 because the credit chain is complete and verifiable with two names, whereas B018 cannot be cited without leaving out the HgTe proposal. On your remaining point, I am satisfied with the maturity of B012, since independent clocks agree at 10^-18, and I would not insist on a realised fundamental-physics result or the redefinition of the second before awarding. I still defer to you and the astrophysicists on B013 and B055.

uncertainties: Whether the lattice-clock community regards Katori and Ye as the right two names, given Lemonde, Ludlow, Takamoto, Bloom and the PTB, NIST and SYRTE groups; an external expert report would help.
Whether the committee accepts a citation built around the magic-wavelength lattice and the 10^-18 result as distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
Whether I am underweighting B018 because of attribution when the physics case is stronger than that of a clock. A two-part prize is not feasible here without cutting names.
I rely on colleagues for the clock community's view of credit and for particle and astroparticle physics (B055, B013).
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile. I have no known connection to Katori, Ye or their institutions, nor to Kane, Mele or Molenkamp. I am a theorist of magnetism and electronic structure, which is a matter of expertise and does not call for recusal, and I am close to condensed-matter topics, not to atomic clocks. I have noted Kroll's Boulder year and Johansson's possible recusal on superconducting-circuit candidates, neither of which affects B012.
